summary: An official public record of an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society concerning the ONC RPC and XDR protocols. It is a legal and administrative document rather than a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC records an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society about ONC RPC and XDR. It grants specified rights for standards work and describes conditions for later implementation licenses.

subtitle: The public record of an agreement about ONC RPC and XDR entering the Internet standards process.

tldr.problem: The Internet Society and IETF needed rights from Sun to use and modify the ONC RPC and XDR specifications for possible standardization.
tldr.mechanism: Sun grants the named Licensees a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license for work intended to make the technology an Internet standard.
tldr.outcome: The agreement says Sun will offer similar no-charge terms to implementers if the technology reaches Proposed Standard, and its evolution license ends if that does not happen within 24 months.

facts.label: Time limit for Proposed Standard status

today: RFC 1790 is an Informational record of a 1995 agreement, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. It is a legal record, not a technical specification.

sections.title: An Agreement, Not a Protocol Standard
sections.content:
RFC 1790 explicitly says it is not a standard. It is the public record of an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society concerning Sun's Open Network Computing (ONC) Remote Procedure Call (RPC) and External Data Representation (XDR) specifications.

The RFC 1057 and RFC 1014 specifications are incorporated by reference but are not attached. The agreement is intended to permit the technology to enter the Internet standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: This document records a legal agreement, not technical rules for using RPC or XDR. It gives the Internet standards process permission to work with those specifications.

sections.title: Rights Granted for Standards Work
sections.content:
Sun grants the Internet Society, the IETF and the named officers, employees, Secretariat and contractors a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license under Sun's rights in the technology. For the purpose of making it an Internet standard, they may use, reproduce, modify, distribute, test, develop, analyze and revise it, create derivative works, and use the marks ONC RPC and ONC XDR.

The agreement also gives the Licensees the exclusive right to evolve and modify the technology through the Internet Standardization Process, as described in RFC 1602. Development outside that process must be identified as non-standard and cannot refer to the Internet Standards Process.
sections.plainLanguage: Sun lets the named Internet organizations use and change the specifications for standards work without charge. Work outside that process must be identified as non-standard.

sections.title: Terms for Other Implementers
sections.content:
The agreement does not require the Licensees to publish or use the technology or move it onto the standards track. If the technology reaches Proposed Standard, Sun agrees to license it to others on substantially similar terms at no charge, provided they implement the Internet standard.

If the technology is not elevated to Proposed Standard within 24 months of the agreement, Section 2 becomes null and void. The introductory note says people or organizations outside the named Licensees need a separate license to use the specifications; Sun commits to offering one under substantially similar terms at no charge.
sections.plainLanguage: The agreement does not force the IETF to publish a standard. If the work reaches Proposed Standard, Sun agrees to offer qualifying implementers similar terms without charge.

sections.title: Other Contract Terms
sections.content:
The agreement provides the technology "as is" and disclaims warranties and liability for specified losses and damages. It says the written agreement replaces earlier agreements on the subject, and that additions or changes must be in writing and signed by authorized representatives.

It also addresses export-control laws and governing law. The signatures are dated 4-6-95 for Sun and 4-11-95 for the Internet Society. The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The agreement also limits warranties and liability and sets rules for written changes. It was signed by representatives of Sun and the Internet Society.
